title: How to Massage: Basic Techniques and a 20-Minute Routine — cv.cm
description: How to massage for beginners: five basic strokes, three pressure levels, how long per area, a 20-minute routine for a friend and a self-massage version.
h1: How do you give a massage? A beginner's guide to the basic techniques
answer: To give a massage, work in a warm room with the person lying comfortably and covered by a towel. Warm a little oil or lotion in your hands, start with slow gliding strokes, then knead the larger muscles, then return to gliding. Keep pressure firm but never painful, stay beside bones and the spine, and ask often whether the pressure feels right.

body: Almost every massage style, from Swedish massage to Chinese tuina, Japanese shiatsu and Thai massage, builds on a few simple movements. You do not need to learn them all at once. Gliding and kneading are enough for a good first massage.

head: Stroke
What you do
Where it works well
Typical time
rows: Long, slow strokes with flat palms, moving toward the heart, then a light return
Back, arms, legs; the start and end of every area
Lift and squeeze the muscle between thumb and fingers, like kneading soft dough, one hand after the other
Top of the shoulders, upper arms, calves, thighs
Small, slow circles with the thumb or fingertips in one spot, moving the skin over the tissue below
Beside the shoulder blades, palms, soles of the feet
Press and hold with a flat palm or thumb, then release slowly
Large muscles of the back and buttocks, the arch of the foot
Gentle, loose tapping with the sides of relaxed hands or cupped palms
Upper back and thighs, only at the end

body: Use your whole hand where you can. Thumbs tire quickly and press harder than you think. Lean your body weight in slowly instead of pushing with your wrists.
Pressure is the part beginners get wrong most often. Think of three levels and use a 1 to 10 scale when you talk about it.

ul: Light (about 2–3 out of 10): your hand moves the skin only. Use it to begin each area, over bony places and for older or fragile people.
Medium (about 4–5 out of 10): your hand moves the muscle under the skin. Most of a home massage should be here.
Firm (about 6 out of 10): deeper, slower pressure that is still comfortable. Use it only on thick muscles, such as the top of the shoulders or the buttocks, and only if the person likes it.

body: Discomfort that feels good is fine. Sharp, burning, electric or shooting pain means stop at once. If the person holds their breath, tenses up or pulls away, you are pressing too hard.

body.note: Agree on words before you start: for example, 'more', 'less' and 'stop'. Ask after the first minute on each new area: 'Is this pressure all right?'

sections.h: Before you start: room, oil and position

ul: Room: warm, about 22–25 °C, with no draft. People cool down quickly when lying still.
Surface: a firm bed or a folded blanket on the floor. A soft sofa makes good pressure hard.
Covering: the person stays clothed or is covered with a large towel or sheet. Uncover only the area you are working on.

Oil or lotion: a plain, unscented oil or lotion. Use about a teaspoon for the back, less for an arm. Warm it in your palms first. Test a small patch of skin first if the person has sensitive skin or allergies, and skip oil on the face.
Support: a pillow under the ankles when lying face down, and under the knees when lying face up. A rolled towel under the forehead keeps the neck straight.
Your hands: short nails, no rings or watch, warm hands.

body: Ask before you begin whether the person has any injury, pain, recent surgery, a blood clot history, a bleeding disorder or takes blood thinners, is pregnant, or has another health condition. If yes, read our page on when not to massage first. For pregnancy, refer to a midwife or doctor and a qualified prenatal therapist.

sections.h: A 20-minute routine for a family member or friend
body: This routine follows a simple order: back and shoulders while the person lies face down, then arms, hands and feet while they lie face up. Set a timer for each step. For example, cv.cm's countdown timer can time each block so you do not spend all your time on one area.

head: Step
What to do
Time
rows: Rest both palms flat on the upper back. Ask about pressure words. Spread oil with slow gliding strokes over the whole back.
Hands flat on each side of the spine, glide up to the shoulders, out over the shoulder blades and lightly down the sides. Repeat slowly.
Knead the muscles on one side of the spine, two finger-widths away from it, from the waist to the shoulder blade. Then the other side.
Knead the top of the shoulders between thumb and fingers. Make small thumb circles around, not on, the edge of each shoulder blade.
Long gliding strokes, then 20 seconds of light tapping on the upper back if the person likes it. Cover the back.
Person turns face up. Glide from wrist to shoulder, then knead the upper arm and forearm. Both arms.
Thumb circles across the palm, then gently slide along each finger from base to tip. Both hands.
Hold one foot in both hands. Glide over the top, press thumb circles along the sole and arch, then circle the ankle slowly. Both feet.
Rest your hands still on the feet or shoulders for a few breaths. Let the person sit up slowly and drink some water if they want.

body: Keep one hand in contact with the body as you move from area to area. Slow, even rhythm matters more than complex technique. If you only have 10 minutes, do steps 1 to 5.
You cannot reach your own back well with your hands, but you can massage most other areas. Sit upright in a chair with both feet on the floor.

ol: Shoulders, 2 minutes: reach your right hand across to your left shoulder. Squeeze the muscle on top between your fingers and the heel of your hand, then make small circles. Switch sides.
Back of the neck, 1 minute: with your fingertips on both sides of the neck, not on the bones in the middle, make slow circles from the base of the skull down to the shoulders.
Forearms, 2 minutes: glide your thumb from the wrist to the elbow on the inside and the outside of each forearm.
Hands, 2 minutes: press thumb circles over the opposite palm and the fleshy base of the thumb. Slide along each finger.
Feet, 3 minutes: rest one foot on the opposite knee and press thumb circles along the sole, or roll the sole slowly over a tennis ball on the floor.

body: For a stiff upper back, lean against a wall with a tennis ball between the wall and the muscle beside your shoulder blade, never on the spine itself.

The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) says the risk of harm from massage appears to be low. Research suggests it may help some kinds of pain, such as neck and shoulder pain, but benefits often last only a short time. A Cochrane review of massage for low back pain found short-term improvements in pain, but the authors had very little confidence in the overall evidence.

Many people find massage relaxing and say it eases muscle tension. That is a reasonable goal for a home massage. Massage is not a treatment for disease, and NCCIH advises not to use it to delay seeing a health professional about a medical problem.

sections.h: What not to press, when to stop and common mistakes

ul: Never press directly on the spine, the front or sides of the neck, the throat, the eyes or the back of the knee.
Avoid broken, infected or sunburned skin, rashes, fresh bruises, swelling and recent injuries.
Use light pressure only over varicose veins, bony areas and on people with osteoporosis, on blood thinners or with a bleeding disorder.
Never massage a calf that is swollen, warm, red or painful on one side. It can be a sign of a blood clot. Get medical help the same day instead.
Stop and seek medical help if the person feels chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, numbness, weakness or dizziness during or after the massage.

head: Mistake
Fix
rows: Pressing too hard, so the person is sore the next day
Halve the pressure and the time on that area next time. Mild soreness should fade within a day or two.
Use flat palms and lean in with body weight; save thumbs for small spots.
Slow down to about one long stroke every 3–4 seconds.
Stay on muscle: two finger-widths beside the spine, around the shoulder blade, not on it.
Check pressure on every new area and whenever the person moves or tenses.

faq.q: Should you massage toward the heart?
faq.a: Long gliding strokes on the arms and legs are traditionally done toward the heart, with a lighter stroke back. For a relaxing home massage the direction matters less than slow speed and comfortable pressure.

faq.q: How long should a massage last?
faq.a: A home massage of 15–30 minutes is plenty. About 3–5 minutes per area, such as the back, shoulders or feet, is enough to feel relaxed without leaving the muscles sore.

faq.q: Is it better to use oil or lotion?
faq.a: Either works. Oil glides longer and suits the back and legs, while lotion absorbs faster and suits hands and feet. Choose an unscented product and test it on a small patch of skin if the person has sensitive skin.

faq.q: Why do I feel sore after a massage?
faq.a: Mild tenderness for a day or two is common, especially after firm pressure. Pain that is severe, gets worse, or comes with swelling, bruising or numbness is not normal and should be checked by a doctor.

faq.q: Can I massage someone every day?
faq.a: Gentle massage every day is usually fine for a healthy adult. Keep firm pressure for every few days, and skip any area that is still tender from the last session.
